summary: This experimental specification proposes a protocol for creating symmetric encryption keys shared by a whole group and for handing them out to the peers who need them. It is the protocol companion to the architecture described in RFC 2094.

eli5.summary: A club leader makes one secret code for the whole club and quietly gives a copy to each member.

questions: how to distribute a shared key to a group
what is the group key management protocol
what is a group controller in gkmp
subtitle: An experimental protocol for creating one shared secret key for a whole group and handing it to each member.

tldr.problem: Existing cooperative key management only produced pairwise keys between two parties, but secure communication by a whole group needs everyone to hold the same key.
tldr.mechanism: A group controller creates two group keys together with a first member, then sets up a one-time session key with each other member and uses it to download the group keys, with signed permissions checked along the way.
tldr.outcome: The protocol also covers rekeying, member-initiated joins and member deletion, but it is only an Experimental RFC and not an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2093 is an Experimental RFC that, in its own words, does not specify an Internet standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Group Keys
sections.content:
The memo says traditional key distribution copied the military paper-based key accounting system: keys were distributed, ordered and accounted for physically, with long lead times and high cost. Cooperative algorithms can generate pairwise keys between two machines, but only pairwise keys were supported.

The Group Key Management Protocol (GKMP) creates keys for cryptographic groups of more than two members and distributes them. Its advertised advantages are that it is nearly invisible to the operator, needs no central key distribution site, gives the key only to group members, works sender or receiver oriented, and can use multicast. It is an application layer protocol and is independent of the underlying communication protocol.
sections.eli5: Normally two friends can agree on a secret code. This protocol lets a whole group share one code without a central code office.

sections.title: Roles and Trust Mechanisms
sections.content:
There are two roles. The group controller (GC) creates and distributes the key, forms the key distribution messages and collects acknowledgments. Every other host in the group is a group member: it helps create keys, checks that the controller is authorized, accepts keys, keeps a local compromise list and reviews key management actions. Any member can become the controller when assigned, because a group must stay on the same key and only one host should rekey at a time.

Access control uses permission certificates signed by a higher authority, so each entity can verify another's permissions but cannot change them. If a peer's permissions do not equal or exceed the service requested, the service is denied. A Compromise Recovery List of compromised entities is carried along, with its version number passed in key management actions, so members can drop connections with them.
sections.eli5: One person is the leader and hands out the code. Everyone carries a signed badge showing what they are allowed to do, and a list of banned people is shared too.

sections.title: Data Items and Messages
sections.content:
The RFC defines a set of data item primitives and builds its messages from them. The group token is created by the authority that commands a group. It carries the group identification, the GC ID, the group action (create, rekey or delete), the group permissions, the rekey interval, a token version, a signature and the commander's public key.

Other primitives include the group traffic encryption key ID (GTEK ID), the group key encryption key ID (GKEK ID), creation fields to which each side contributes, distributor and member signatures, and the encrypted group keys. The message definitions include Create Grp Keys_1 and _2, Negotiate Grp Keys_1 and _2, Create Session KEK_1 and _2, Download Grp Keys, Key download ack, Rekey_Multicast, Request_Group_Join, Delete_Group_Keys and Grp_Keys_Deleted_Ack. Messages that carry permissions are encrypted because they may be sensitive. The protocol also defines thirteen states, each a short checklist such as checking the CRL, validating the token and comparing permissions.
sections.eli5: The messages are like notes passed between the leader and a member, each stamped with a signature and some locked in a code so nobody else can read them.

sections.title: Creating a Group and Distributing Keys
sections.content:
Group creation starts when some entity sends a signed command to the GC. The GC then works with the first member to create two keys: the group traffic encryption key (GTEK) and the group key encryption key (GKEK). The RFC explains that two hosts cooperate because one host could only make a good key with a trusted random function, which usually needs specialized hardware. Four messages pass between the GC and the first member, and the GC sends its final negotiation message encrypted in the GTEK it just generated.

The other members then get the keys. The GC and each member first create a one-time session key encryption key (SKEK). The two sides exchange permissions and the CRL version number, and the GC sends the keys in a Download Grp Keys message encrypted in the SKEK. The member checks the group ID, GC ID and permissions, updates its key tables and acknowledges. This takes six messages per member.
sections.eli5: The leader and one helper mix their secrets to make the club codes. Then the leader whispers the codes to each other member through a private channel set up just for that person.

sections.title: Rekeying, Joining and Leaving
sections.content:
Rekey reuses the first-member exchange to make a new GTEK and GKEK. The GC then sends one signed Rekey_Multicast message, encrypted in the GKEK that all members already hold, so a single message can reach the whole group. Members decrypt and validate it, then update their key tables.

In a member initiated join the joining member first sends Request_Group_Join. The GC decides based on group parameters such as membership limits and lists, and the rest matches the normal key distribution, for seven messages in total. The RFC gives an example of a corporation keeping job vacancy announcements encrypted. Where even the fact of joining is sensitive, a pairwise key may be created first to hide the request.

Cooperative deletion uses a Delete_Group_Keys message encrypted in the GTEK, and the member deletes its keys and sends an acknowledgment. Hostile deletion assumes the member's keys are lost, so the GC creates a new group without that member, switches group operations to it, and cancels the old group by several multicasts of a group delete message.
sections.eli5: To change the club code, the leader announces the new one using the old one. To add someone, they ask to join first. To remove a trusted friend, the leader just asks them to throw away their copy; for a bad actor, the club starts over with a new code.

sections.title: Compromise and Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC's Security section is one line: the document in its entirety concerns security. In the section on compromise, the RFC admits a trade-off. From a security view, all traffic should stop when a member is found to be bad, but if that traffic supports a critical operation, the group may prefer to live with the leak instead.

The GKMP provides two mechanisms to restrict compromised members. It checks a revocation list during group creation, so a compromised member is not included in a new group, and it makes it possible to create another group without the compromised members. It does not dictate whether the old group may continue to operate with a compromised member.
sections.eli5: If someone untrustworthy learns the club code, the club can change it, but sometimes the club has to decide whether stopping everything is worth it.
